summary:
**Project Merobiman** is an interactive Earth observation prototype that makes environmental data easier to explore and understand. Built with React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS and Go, it uses MapLibre and OpenStreetMap to display data on an interactive globe.

Using NASA GISTEMP temperature records, users can select a region and time period, visualize temperature changes, and examine a trend’s magnitude, uncertainty and p-value. The prototype also displays wind and ocean-current snapshots, alongside satellite imagery of aerosols, ocean chlorophyll and vegetation. These additional layers provide context but do not yet support quantitative trend analysis.

Merobiman aims to help students, researchers and communities turn complex Earth science data into accessible evidence for learning and informed environmental discussions.
details:
Project Merobiman

Merobiman is a map-first Earth science prototype that helps users explore environmental data and investigate how temperature has changed over time. Rather than presenting disconnected charts, it places the investigation on an interactive globe, where users can select a region and time period and see results in geographic context.

How it works

For temperature analysis, Merobiman uses NASA’s GISTEMP land–ocean temperature dataset. Users can choose a preset region, draw a rectangle on the map or enter coordinates. The application calculates a regional annual temperature-anomaly series and estimates the trend over the selected period.

It also presents uncertainty and statistical-significance information, including a p-value, helping users distinguish the size of a change from the strength of the evidence. Results can be exported as CSV or JSON.

The prototype displays wind and ocean-current snapshots using vector arrows and animated particles. Satellite imagery adds context through aerosol optical depth, ocean chlorophyll and vegetation indicators. These layers support visual exploration but do not yet provide numerical trend or significance analysis.

Tools and development

The frontend was built with React, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS. MapLibre provides globe and flat-map views, with OpenStreetMap as the basemap. A Go backend processes temperature data, calculates regional trends and serves the application. The prototype runs locally on a computer and requires no specialized hardware.

Benefits and intended impact

Merobiman aims to make scientific data more approachable for students, researchers and communities. By combining maps, historical observations, statistical context and downloadable results, it helps users ask informed questions about where change is occurring and how confidently it can be measured.

Its intended impact is to support environmental learning and informed decision-making—not to replace expert analysis or establish the cause of a particular change.

Creativity and design considerations

Merobiman makes Earth itself the starting point for investigation: users explore a location on the map before examining its data. It also connects temperature trends with visual context from other Earth systems.

Scientific transparency was a key consideration. The prototype identifies data sources and limitations, treats missing observations as missing rather than zero, and does not present imagery as precise pollution measurements. It also shows uncertainty in temperature trends and includes accessible controls, reduced-motion support and mobile layouts.
